2.title: Living Stones and Holy Exiles: Identity, Witness, and the Suffering Christ
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves from who Christians are (vv. 1–10) to how they live in a hostile world (vv. 11–25). You are living stones in God’s house, a chosen race, a royal priesthood; therefore live so well among unbelievers that those who slander you will glorify God. Identity produces conduct, and conduct commends the identity.

The chapter ends with Christ’s unjust suffering (vv. 18–25). Peter frames submission not as mere social conformity but as following the suffering Servant, who entrusted himself to God, and then did what no one else could: bore our sins in his body on the tree.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Living Stones, a Royal Priesthood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Put off the sins that destroy love, and crave the pure milk of God’s word. Come to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but precious to God, and be built with other believers into one spiritual house and holy priesthood. Christ is the cornerstone to those who believe and a stumbling stone to those who disobey. And believers are now given Israel’s titles: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people, called to declare his excellencies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priesthood of All Believers

Coming to Christ, the living stone, believers are built into one spiritual house and a holy priesthood, offering sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel’s titles were given to Gentile converts with no status at all.

Now: Once not a people, now God’s people; once without mercy, now shown mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation— if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.

Meaning first. 1 Peter 2 tells God’s new people who they are and how they should live in a hostile world. Born again by the word (1:23), they must strip off malice and deceit and crave the pure milk of the word, so that they grow (vv. 1–3). They are coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, and they themselves are living stones being built into a spiritual temple and a holy priesthood (vv. 4–5). Scripture foretold this cornerstone: those who believe will never be put to shame, but those who disobey the word stumble over him (vv. 6–8). They are now what Israel was called to be: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s own people, called out of darkness to declare his praises (vv. 9–10). So, as exiles, they must abstain from sinful desires and live such good lives among unbelievers that slanderers will glorify God (vv. 11–12). They must submit to human authorities for the Lord’s sake, living as free people and servants of God, honouring everyone, loving believers, fearing God and honouring the emperor (vv. 13–17). Slaves must submit even to harsh masters, because suffering for doing good is commendable before God (vv. 18–20). For Christ suffered for us, leaving an example: he committed no sin, did not retaliate, entrusted himself to God, and bore our sins in his body on the cross, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness; by his wounds we are healed; we were straying sheep, but have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of our souls (vv. 21–25).

So put away all malice. Key words. “So” (oun, therefore): because you have been born again and are called to love (1:22–23). “Put away” (apothemenoi, strip off, as dirty clothes), as in James 1:21. “Malice” (kakian, ill will, wickedness).

And all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander. Key words. “Deceit” (dolon, trickery, guile, like bait on a hook). “Hypocrisy” (hypokriseis, play-acting, pretence). “Envy” (phthonous, jealousy). “Slander” (katalalias, evil speaking, backbiting), as in James 4:11. All sins that destroy the brotherly love just commanded (1:22). Note: “all” three times. Strip off every trace.

Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk. Key words. “Newborn infants” (artigennēta brephē, just-born babies). “Long for” (epipothēsate, crave, yearn intensely). A newborn baby craves milk with all its being. “Pure” (adolon, without guile, unadulterated), a wordplay with “deceit” (dolon) in verse 1. “Spiritual” (logikon, of the word, reasonable, rational): the milk of the word of God (1:23–25). The word is the believer’s nourishment.

That by it you may grow up into salvation. Key words. “Grow up” (auxēthēte, be increased, mature). “Into salvation”: toward its final completion (1:5, 9). Growth through the word is the path to final salvation.

If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good. Key words. From Psalm 34:8: “Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good!” “Tasted” (egeusasthe, experienced). “The Lord”: in Psalm 34, Yahweh; here applied to Christ (v. 4). “Good” (chrēstos, kind, gracious; sounding like Christos). If you have tasted Christ’s goodness, you will crave more of him.

What it does not mean. “Milk” here does not mean elementary teaching, as in Hebrews 5:12–13 and 1 Corinthians 3:2. Here it refers to the whole word of God, which all believers, mature or young, must crave as eagerly as a baby craves milk.

In a sentence. Therefore, get rid of all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander of every kind. Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation, now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.

On a Tuesday. Do you crave God’s word like a hungry baby craves milk? If not, ask God to increase your appetite, and feed on it daily this week.

verseByVerse.quote: As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

As you come to him. Key words. “Come” (proserchomenoi, approach, draw near, present tense: keep coming). The word used for approaching God in worship (Hebrews 4:16; 10:22). The Christian life is continual coming to Christ.

A living stone rejected by men. Key words. “Living stone” (lithon zōnta): a paradox. Stones are dead; Christ is a living stone because he is risen. “Rejected” (apodedokimasmenon, tested and rejected, declared unfit after examination), from Psalm 118:22. The religious leaders examined Jesus and threw him out (Mark 8:31; 12:10).

But in the sight of God chosen and precious. Key words. “Chosen” (eklekton) and “precious” (entimon, honoured, valuable), from Isaiah 28:16. Men rejected him; God chose and honoured him.

You yourselves like living stones. Key words. Believers share Christ’s life; they too are living stones. Peter (whose name means “rock”) does not claim to be the foundation stone; Christ is. All believers are stones built on him.

Are being built up as a spiritual house. Key words. “Being built” (oikodomeisthe, present tense: God is building). “Spiritual house” (oikos pneumatikos): a temple, made of people, indwelt by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Corinthians 3:16). The Jerusalem temple was made of dead stones; God’s new temple is made of living people.

To be a holy priesthood. Key words. “Priesthood” (hierateuma, body of priests). Not some believers, but all. Every believer is a priest with direct access to God (Revelation 1:6; 5:10).

To offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Key words. “Spiritual sacrifices”: not animals, but praise (Hebrews 13:15), good works and generosity (Hebrews 13:16), our whole lives (Romans 12:1), prayer (Revelation 8:3–4). “Acceptable” (euprosdektous, well-pleasing). “Through Jesus Christ”: only through him, our High Priest, are our offerings accepted.

Where Christians differ: is there a special priesthood in the church? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches maintain an ordained priesthood that offers sacrifice on behalf of the people. Verdict: The New Testament teaches the priesthood of all believers. Every Christian is a priest, offering spiritual sacrifices directly to God through Christ, the one great High Priest. The church has elders and deacons, who lead and serve, but no priestly caste that mediates between God and the people (1 Timothy 2:5). Peter himself, the first leader of the apostles, describes himself as a fellow elder (5:1), and Christ, not Peter, as the stone on which the church is built.

What it does not mean. The priesthood of all believers does not mean there is no church leadership or no ordered ministry. God gives elders to teach and shepherd (5:1–4; Ephesians 4:11). It means no believer needs another human being to approach God for them.

In a sentence. As you come to him, the living Stone, rejected by people but chosen by God and precious to him, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

For worship. Come to Christ today as a priest: offer him your praise, your prayer, your work, your whole self.

verseByVerse.quote: For it stands in Scripture: "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame." So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone," and "A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense." They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it stands in Scripture: “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” and “A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.” They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do.

For it stands in Scripture. Key words. Three stone passages follow, from Isaiah and the Psalms.

Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious. Key words. From Isaiah 28:16. “Cornerstone” (akrogōniaion, the chief corner stone, the foundation stone that sets the lines of the whole building). God himself laid it.

And whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. Key words. “Believes in him”: Isaiah’s stone is a person. “Put to shame” (kataischynthē, disappointed, humiliated). Those who trust Christ will never be let down, now or at the judgement (Romans 9:33; 10:11).

So the honor is for you who believe. Key words. “Honor” (timē, preciousness, value): related to “precious” (entimon). The preciousness of Christ belongs to believers; they share his honour.

But for those who do not believe, The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Key words. From Psalm 118:22, quoted by Jesus himself (Matthew 21:42) and by Peter before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:11). The builders (the religious leaders) rejected him, but God made him the chief stone. Unbelief cannot overturn God’s choice.

And A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense. Key words. From Isaiah 8:14. “Stumbling” (proskommatos) and “offense” (skandalou, a trap, a snare, a cause of falling). For unbelievers, Christ is not a foundation but an obstacle; they trip over him to their ruin (1 Corinthians 1:23).

They stumble because they disobey the word. Key words. “Disobey” (apeithountes, refuse to believe, refuse to be persuaded). Unbelief is disobedience to the gospel. The cause of stumbling is their own refusal.

As they were destined to do. Key words. “Destined” (etethēsan, appointed, placed). God appointed that those who disobey the word would stumble. Their stumbling is both their own guilty choice and within God’s sovereign purpose.

Where Christians differ: does God destine people to unbelief? Some read this as teaching only that God appointed the consequence (stumbling) for those who freely choose to disobey. Verdict: The verse teaches that those who disobey stumble according to God’s appointment. God is sovereign over all things, including the rejection of Christ by unbelievers (Romans 9:18–22; Acts 4:27–28). Yet the stumbling is caused by their own disobedience, for which they are wholly responsible. God passes over some, leaving them in their sin, and justly appoints them to its consequences; he does not create unbelief in an innocent heart. The doctrine is to be handled with humility and reverence, not speculation, and it is set against the glory of the chosen in the next verse.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone is prevented from believing who wants to believe. Whoever believes will not be put to shame. Unbelief is always a guilty refusal.

In a sentence. For Scripture says: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a chosen and precious cornerstone, and the one who trusts in him will never be put to shame.” Now to you who believe, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone,” and, “A stone that causes people to stumble and a rock that makes them fall.” They stumble because they disobey the message, which is also what they were destined for.

For worship. Thank God that Christ is precious to you, the cornerstone of your life, and pray for those who are stumbling over him.

verseByVerse.quote: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

But you are a chosen race. Key words. “But you”: in contrast with those who stumble. Titles once given to Israel at Sinai are now given to the church (Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 7:6; Isaiah 43:20–21). “Chosen race” (genos eklekton): a new people, not by physical descent but by God’s choice.

A royal priesthood. Key words. “Royal priesthood” (basileion hierateuma), from Exodus 19:6, “a kingdom of priests.” Priests who belong to the King, and who share his reign (Revelation 1:6; 5:10).

A holy nation. Key words. “Nation” (ethnos). Set apart for God, drawn from every nation.

A people for his own possession. Key words. “His own possession” (laos eis peripoiēsin, a people acquired, treasured), as in Titus 2:14 and Exodus 19:5 (“my treasured possession”). God’s special treasure.

That you may proclaim the excellencies of him. Key words. “Proclaim” (exangeilēte, announce, publish, declare out loud). “Excellencies” (aretas, virtues, praises, mighty deeds). The purpose of God’s people: to make known his greatness to the world (Isaiah 43:21).

Who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. Key words. “Called” (kalesantos): God’s effectual call. “Darkness”: ignorance, sin, the realm of Satan (Acts 26:18; Colossians 1:13). “Marvelous light” (thaumaston phōs, wonderful light): the light of God’s truth and presence. A total transfer.

Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people. Key words. From Hosea 1:9–10; 2:23. God named Hosea’s child “Not my people” as a sign of Israel’s rejection, then promised to restore them. Paul applies the same passage to Gentiles (Romans 9:25–26). Gentiles who were not God’s people are now his people.

Once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy. Key words. Hosea’s daughter was named “No Mercy” (Hosea 1:6). Now mercy has come.

Where Christians differ: is the church a replacement for Israel, or are they two separate peoples? Dispensationalists keep Israel and the church as two distinct peoples with distinct promises; some speak of “replacement theology” in which the church replaces Israel entirely. Verdict: Peter applies Israel’s titles directly to the mostly Gentile church. The church is not a separate people from Israel but the fulfilment of God’s purpose for Israel: one people of God, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, the true seed of Abraham (Galatians 3:29; Ephesians 2:11–22; Romans 11:17–24). This is fulfilment, not mere replacement: believing Jews were the core of the church, and God continues to graft Jews back in through faith in Christ (Romans 11:23–26).

What it does not mean. It does not make the church an ethnic or national people. It is a spiritual people from every nation. Nor does it mean believers may be proud; they were chosen by mercy alone.

In a sentence. But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God’s special possession, so that you may declare the praises of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.

For worship. Read this verse aloud as your identity. Then declare God’s praises to someone this week.
verseByVerse.note: Titles once given to Israel at Sinai are now given to the church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–25 — Submission, and the Steps of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As foreigners and exiles, fight the desires that war against your soul, and live so well among unbelievers that their slander is silenced and they glorify God. Submit for the Lord’s sake to every human authority, even the emperor. Live as free people, as God’s servants. Slaves, submit even to unjust masters, because Christ suffered unjustly, leaving an example to trace. He did not retaliate, but entrusted himself to God. And he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.theology:
Entrusting Rather Than Suppressing

Christ did not revile in return; he kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly. Then he did what no follower can copy: he bore our sins in his body on the tree.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter spoke directly to slaves, and told believers to honour an emperor who would soon persecute them.

Now: Follow in his steps: do good, bear injustice without retaliation, and hand the case to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation.

Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles. Key words. “Beloved” (agapētoi). “Urge” (parakalō, appeal, exhort). “Sojourners” (paroikous, resident aliens) and “exiles” (parepidēmous, temporary residents), as in 1:1, 17. Your identity shapes your conduct: you do not belong here, so do not live like those who do.

To abstain from the passions of the flesh. Key words. “Abstain” (apechesthai, keep away from, hold yourself back). “Passions of the flesh” (sarkikōn epithymiōn, desires of sinful human nature): sexual sin, greed, gluttony, anger, pride (Galatians 5:19–21).

Which wage war against your soul. Key words. “Wage war” (strateuontai, campaign, fight as soldiers), as in James 4:1. Sinful desires are not harmless pleasures but enemy soldiers attacking your soul. They seek your destruction.

Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable. Key words. “Gentiles” (ethnesin): here meaning unbelievers, the surrounding pagan society. Peter’s mostly Gentile readers are now the true Israel; the unbelieving world is “the Gentiles.” “Honorable” (kalēn, good, beautiful, attractive).

So that when they speak against you as evildoers. Key words. “Speak against” (katalalousin, slander). Early Christians were accused of atheism (rejecting the gods), cannibalism (misunderstanding the Lord’s Supper), incest (calling each other brother and sister), and disloyalty to Rome (refusing to worship the emperor).

They may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation. Key words. “See” (epopteuontes, observe closely, watch over time). “Good deeds” (kalōn ergōn). Jesus said the same (Matthew 5:16). “Day of visitation” (hēmera episkopēs): the day God comes, either in salvation (when the slanderers are converted and then glorify God) or in judgement (when they are forced to acknowledge God’s people were right). Probably the first: good lives can win slanderers to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good conduct will always prevent persecution. Jesus lived perfectly and was crucified. But good conduct removes legitimate grounds for accusation and can lead others to faith.

In a sentence. Dear friends, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to keep away from the sinful desires that wage war against your soul. Live such good lives among the unbelievers around you that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us.

On a Tuesday. Is there a neighbour or colleague who thinks badly of Christians? Let your good deeds this week give them reason to think again.

verseByVerse.quote: Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people.

Be subject for the Lord’s sake. Key words. “Be subject” (hypotagēte, submit, place yourselves under). A key word in this section (2:13, 18; 3:1, 5). “For the Lord’s sake”: the motive is not fear of government, but loyalty to Christ, who wants his people to honour God-given authority (Romans 13:1–7).

To every human institution. Key words. “Human institution” (anthrōpinē ktisei, human creation, human authority structure). Government is a human arrangement, but ordained by God.

Whether it be to the emperor as supreme. Key words. “Emperor” (basilei, king). The emperor at the time was probably Nero, who would soon persecute Christians and, according to tradition, have Peter crucified. Yet Peter calls for submission. “Supreme” (hyperechonti, highest authority).

Or to governors as sent by him. Key words. Provincial governors, like Pilate, Felix and Festus.

To punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. Key words. The purpose of government: justice, restraining evil and rewarding good (Romans 13:3–4). Even imperfect government serves this purpose to a degree.

For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people. Key words. “Put to silence” (phimoun, muzzle, gag). “Ignorance” (agnōsian, lack of knowledge). “Foolish” (aphronōn, senseless). Good citizenship silences slanderous accusations that Christians are subversive.

Where Christians differ: when may Christians disobey the government? Verdict: Christians must submit to governing authorities as a general rule, paying taxes, obeying laws and honouring officials (Romans 13:1–7). But when the government commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, believers must obey God rather than men (Acts 4:19–20; 5:29; Daniel 3; 6). Even then, they should accept the consequences peacefully, without violent rebellion, as Peter and the apostles did. Christians may also work through lawful means to change unjust laws.

What it does not mean. It does not mean governments are always right, or that Christians must approve of everything rulers do. It means our basic posture is respect and submission, for the Lord’s sake.

In a sentence. For the Lord’s sake, submit to every human authority: whether to the emperor, as the supreme authority, or to governors, who are sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to commend those who do right. For it is God’s will that by doing good you should silence the ignorant talk of foolish people.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your government leaders by name this week, and obey the laws faithfully as service to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The emperor at the time was probably Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor.

Live as people who are free. Key words. “Free” (eleutheroi). Christians are truly free: free from sin’s slavery, from the law’s condemnation, from fear of man (John 8:36; Galatians 5:1). Submission to authorities is not slavery but the free choice of those who serve God.

Not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil. Key words. “Cover-up” (epikalymma, veil, pretext, cloak). Some might use Christian freedom as an excuse to disobey authorities or to indulge sin (Galatians 5:13; Jude 4).

But living as servants of God. Key words. “Servants” (douloi, slaves). The paradox: true freedom is slavery to God (Romans 6:22). We are free from everything else in order to serve him.

Honor everyone. Key words. Four short commands. “Honor” (timēsate, value, respect). Every human being, made in God’s image, deserves respect, including slaves, pagans and enemies.

Love the brotherhood. Key words. “Brotherhood” (adelphotēta, the family of believers). Respect for all; love for the family.

Fear God. Key words. “Fear” (phobeisthe, revere). God alone is to be feared in the highest sense (Proverbs 1:7).

Honor the emperor. Key words. “Honor” (timate). The same word used for “honor everyone.” The emperor receives honour, as all people do, but not fear or worship. Only God is feared. Christians would not offer incense to the emperor as a god, but they would respect him as a ruler. This is the balance (Proverbs 24:21; Matthew 22:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must agree with or admire every leader. It means they show proper respect for the office and the person, while giving ultimate allegiance to God alone.

In a sentence. Live as free people, but do not use your freedom as a cover for evil; live as God’s slaves. Show proper respect to everyone, love the family of believers, fear God, honour the emperor.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you have failed to honour, a leader, a colleague, a stranger? Show them respect this week, as one made in God’s image.

verseByVerse.quote: Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God.

Servants, be subject to your masters with all respect. Key words. “Servants” (oiketai, household slaves, domestic servants). Many early believers were slaves. On slavery and Scripture, see 1 Timothy 6:1–2. “Respect” (phobō, fear, reverence), perhaps reverence toward God shown in how they serve.

Not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust. Key words. “Good” (agathois) and “gentle” (epieikesin, reasonable, kind). “Unjust” (skoliois, crooked, harsh, perverse; our word “scoliosis”). Submission is not conditional on the master being kind.

For this is a gracious thing. Key words. “Gracious thing” (charis, grace, favour, something commendable, that God approves). Patient endurance of unjust suffering finds favour with God.

When, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. Key words. “Mindful of God” (dia syneidēsin theou, because of conscience toward God, being conscious of God). The motive is awareness of God and his will. “Endures” (hypopherei, bears up under). “Sorrows” (lypas, pains, griefs). “Unjustly” (adikōs, undeservedly).

For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? Key words. “Credit” (kleos, glory, fame, praise). “Beaten” (kolaphizomenoi, struck with the fist, buffeted), the word used of the soldiers beating Jesus (Matthew 26:67). Enduring deserved punishment earns no praise.

But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God. Key words. Suffering for doing right, without retaliation, pleases God. It reflects Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not endorse slavery, abuse or injustice. Nor does it forbid escaping abuse when possible (1 Corinthians 7:21), or seeking legal protection (Acts 16:37; 22:25). It addresses how believers should respond when they cannot escape unjust suffering: with patient endurance, trusting God, not with revenge. Victims of domestic abuse are not commanded to remain in danger.

In a sentence. Slaves, in reverent fear of God submit yourselves to your masters, not only to those who are good and considerate, but also to those who are harsh. For it is commendable if someone bears up under the pain of unjust suffering because they are conscious of God. But how is it to your credit if you receive a beating for doing wrong and endure it? But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.

On a Tuesday. If you face unfair treatment at work this week, respond with patience and integrity, trusting God who sees.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps.

For to this you have been called. Key words. “Called” (eklēthēte): God’s effectual call (1:15; 2:9). “To this”: to patient endurance of unjust suffering. Suffering is part of the Christian calling (Philippians 1:29; 2 Timothy 3:12).

Because Christ also suffered for you. Key words. “Suffered” (epathen). “For you” (hyper hymōn, on your behalf). Christ’s suffering was substitutionary: for us, in our place.

Leaving you an example. Key words. “Example” (hypogrammon, a writing copy, a pattern of letters traced by children learning to write). A teacher would write letters at the top of a page; the student traced them below. Christ wrote the pattern; we trace it.

So that you might follow in his steps. Key words. “Follow” (epakolouthēsēte, follow closely). “Steps” (ichnesin, footprints, tracks). Walk exactly where he walked, placing your feet in his footprints.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is only an example. His death was first a substitution (v. 24), which no one can imitate. But having been saved by his substitution, we follow his example.

In a sentence. This is what you were called to, because Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example to trace, so that you would follow in his footsteps.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he suffered for you. Then ask him to help you trace his pattern of patient love today.

verseByVerse.quote: He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly.

He committed no sin. Key words. From Isaiah 53:9. Peter knew Jesus personally for three years and testifies to his sinlessness (Hebrews 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 John 3:5). His suffering was entirely unjust.

Neither was deceit found in his mouth. Key words. “Deceit” (dolos, guile), as in verse 1. Even under interrogation and torture, he spoke only truth.

When he was reviled, he did not revile in return. Key words. “Reviled” (loidoroumenos, insulted, abused verbally). At his trial and on the cross, he was mocked (Matthew 26:67–68; 27:39–44). He did not answer insult with insult.

When he suffered, he did not threaten. Key words. “Threaten” (ēpeilei, warn of vengeance). He had the power to call down legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), but did not. He prayed for his executioners (Luke 23:34).

But continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Key words. “Continued entrusting” (paredidou, imperfect tense: kept handing over, committing). He handed his case over to God the Father, the righteous Judge (Luke 23:46). That is how he could refrain from retaliation: he trusted God to vindicate him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus never spoke out against evil. He denounced hypocrisy (Matthew 23) and challenged an unjust blow (John 18:23). But he did not retaliate personally or seek revenge.

In a sentence. He never sinned, and no lie was ever found on his lips. When they hurled insults at him, he did not retaliate; when he suffered, he made no threats. Instead, he kept entrusting himself to the one who judges justly.

On a Tuesday. When someone insults or wrongs you this week, do not retaliate. Hand your case to God, who judges justly.

verseByVerse.quote: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.

He himself bore our sins. Key words. “He himself” (autos, emphatic): no one else. “Bore” (anēnenken, carried up, took up, offered up), echoing Isaiah 53:4, 11–12. The word is used of carrying a sacrifice up to an altar. He carried our sins and their penalty (Hebrews 9:28). This is substitutionary atonement: our sins were laid on him, and he bore the punishment we deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6).

In his body on the tree. Key words. “In his body”: really, physically. “Tree” (xylon, wood), the cross. Peter uses the word deliberately (Acts 5:30; 10:39), recalling Deuteronomy 21:23: anyone hanged on a tree is under God’s curse. Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13).

That we might die to sin and live to righteousness. Key words. “Die to sin” (tais hamartiais apogenomenoi, having ceased to exist with respect to sins, having departed from sins). Christ’s death breaks sin’s power over us; we are united with him in his death (Romans 6:2–11). “Live to righteousness”: a new life of obedience. The purpose of the atonement is not only forgiveness but transformation.

By his wounds you have been healed. Key words. From Isaiah 53:5. “Wounds” (mōlōpi, bruise, welt, the swollen mark left by a whip). Slaves who had been beaten (v. 20) would know exactly what this meant. His wounds bring our healing. “Healed” (iathēte): in context, spiritual healing from sin (v. 25 speaks of straying sheep returning).

Where Christians differ: does this verse promise physical healing now? Some teach that physical healing is guaranteed in the atonement, so that believers can claim it now by faith. Verdict: In context, Peter speaks of healing from sin: we were straying, now we have returned; we have died to sin. Christ’s atonement does secure the ultimate healing of our bodies at the resurrection (Romans 8:23; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and God may heal in answer to prayer now (James 5:14–15). But physical healing is not guaranteed in this life; believers still get sick and die. The healing promised now is the healing of the soul.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s death merely shows us how to suffer. It actually removed our sins by bearing their penalty. Penal substitution is at the heart of this verse.

In a sentence. He himself carried our sins in his body on the cross, so that we might die to sins and live for righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he carried your sins in his body on the tree, and that his wounds have healed you.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.

For you were straying like sheep. Key words. From Isaiah 53:6: “All we like sheep have gone astray.” “Straying” (planōmenoi, wandering, lost). Sheep wander without realising the danger. Helpless, defenceless, lost.

But have now returned. Key words. “Returned” (epestraphēte, were turned back, passive). Conversion. They returned because they were turned, by the Shepherd who seeks the lost (Luke 15:3–7).

To the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. Key words. “Shepherd” (poimena): Jesus, the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11) and the Chief Shepherd (5:4). Peter, who had been told “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17), points to the true Shepherd. “Overseer” (episkopon, guardian, bishop): one who watches over and cares for. Jesus is the true Overseer of his people, over all human overseers (5:2–4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the sheep returned by their own initiative. The passive voice shows that they were brought back. Yet they truly returned, by faith and repentance.

In a sentence. For you were like sheep going astray, but now you have been brought back to the Shepherd and Guardian of your souls.

For worship. Thank Jesus, your Shepherd and Guardian, who found you when you were lost and watches over your soul today.

3.title: Suffering for Righteousness: Wives, Husbands, and Christ's Victory
3.overview: Chapter 3 completes the household instructions for wives and husbands (vv. 1–7), calls the whole church to repay evil with blessing and to give a gentle reason for its hope (vv. 8–17), and grounds everything in Christ (vv. 18–22): his once-for-all death, his proclamation to the spirits in prison, his resurrection and his ascension to God’s right hand, with every power subject to him. The movement is from the household to the cosmos. Christ’s victory over every power is the ground for enduring any unjust suffering.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wives are to submit to their own husbands, so that unbelieving husbands may be won by their lives. Their beauty should be inward, a gentle and quiet spirit, precious to God, like the holy women of old who hoped in God and did not give way to fear. Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding, honouring them as fellow heirs of the grace of life, so that their prayers are not hindered.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading This Passage Rightly

The Christ-pattern applies to wives and husbands alike. A believing wife may win an unbelieving husband by her conduct; a husband must honour his wife as a fellow heir of the grace of life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A woman converted without her husband was in a precarious position.

Now: This is a text about witness in marriage, never about tolerating abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives, when they see your respectful and pure conduct.

Meaning first. 1 Peter 3 continues the theme of godly submission and suffering. Wives are to submit to their husbands, so that unbelieving husbands may be won by their pure and respectful lives rather than by words; their beauty should be the inner beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, as with the holy women of old like Sarah (vv. 1–6). Husbands are to live with their wives with understanding and honour, as co-heirs of grace, so that their prayers are not hindered (v. 7). All believers are to be united, sympathetic, loving, tender and humble, never repaying evil for evil but blessing, as Psalm 34 promises those who turn from evil and pursue peace (vv. 8–12). If they suffer for doing right, they are blessed; they need not fear but should honour Christ as Lord in their hearts, always ready to explain their hope with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience so that slanderers are put to shame (vv. 13–17). For Christ himself suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God; put to death in the flesh, he was made alive in the Spirit, in whom he proclaimed to the spirits now in prison who disobeyed in Noah’s day, when only eight were saved through water (vv. 18–20). Baptism, which corresponds to that, now saves, not by washing the body, but as the appeal of a good conscience to God, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and reigns over all powers (vv. 21–22).

Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands. Key words. “Likewise” (homoiōs, in the same way): continuing the theme of submission for the Lord’s sake (2:13, 18). “Be subject” (hypotassomenai, submit, place yourselves under). “Your own husbands” (tois idiois andrasin): not all men, but one’s own husband. A voluntary, respectful following of his lead (Ephesians 5:22–24; Colossians 3:18; Titus 2:5).

So that even if some do not obey the word. Key words. “Do not obey the word” (apeithousin tō logō, disbelieve the gospel). In the ancient world, a wife was expected to follow her husband’s religion. A Christian wife with a pagan husband was in a difficult and potentially dangerous position.

They may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives. Key words. “Won” (kerdēthēsontai, gained, won over, a term used for winning converts, 1 Corinthians 9:19–22). “Without a word” (aneu logou): not by preaching or nagging, but by the silent sermon of a godly life. The gospel word has already been heard and rejected; what may win him now is his wife’s transformed conduct.

When they see your respectful and pure conduct. Key words. “See” (epopteusantes, observe closely, watch over time), as in 2:12. “Respectful” (en phobō, in fear, reverence toward God). “Pure” (hagnēn, chaste, holy).

Where Christians differ: does wifely submission belong only to ancient culture? Egalitarians argue that Peter is giving missionary advice suited to a patriarchal culture, and that mutual submission without distinct roles is the Christian ideal today. Verdict: Peter’s concern is indeed partly missional, but he grounds the instruction in the example of holy women of the Old Testament (v. 5), and Paul grounds it in Christ and the church and in creation (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). The complementarian view holds that husband and wife are equal in worth and co-heirs of grace (v. 7), with distinct roles: the husband leads with sacrificial love, the wife follows with respect and strength. Submission never requires sin (Acts 5:29), never means enduring abuse, and never makes the wife inferior.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a wife must abandon her faith to please her husband. She is to remain a Christian, which itself was a form of non-submission in that culture. Nor does it mean wives must never speak about Christ; it means their lives should do most of the speaking.

In a sentence. In the same way, wives, follow your own husbands’ lead, so that if any of them do not believe the word, they may be won over without words by the behaviour of their wives, when they see the purity and reverence of your lives.

On a Tuesday. Wives with unbelieving husbands: pray daily for your husband, and let your love, respect and joy be your strongest witness.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear— but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious.

Do not let your adorning be external. Key words. “Adorning” (kosmos, ornament, decoration; from which comes “cosmetic”). “External” (exōthen, outward). Not merely outward.

The braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear. Key words. Wealthy Roman women spent hours on elaborate hairstyles woven with gold and jewels, and wore expensive clothing to display status, as in 1 Timothy 2:9.

But let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart. Key words. “Hidden person of the heart” (ho kryptos tēs kardias anthrōpos, the hidden self of the heart): the inner self, character, who you really are.

With the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit. Key words. “Imperishable” (aphthartō), as in 1:4, 23: outward beauty fades; inner beauty lasts forever. “Gentle” (praeōs, meek, humble, not self-assertive). “Quiet” (hēsychiou, calm, peaceful, tranquil, not anxious or agitated). Not a personality type (quiet versus loud) but a heart at rest in God.

Which in God’s sight is very precious. Key words. “Very precious” (polytelēs, very costly, of great value), the word used of expensive perfume (Mark 14:3). God values inner beauty more than all the jewellery in the world.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid braided hair, jewellery or nice clothes entirely; otherwise it would forbid “the clothing you wear” too. It forbids making outward appearance the main focus. Nor does it apply only to women; men too should be adorned with gentleness.

In a sentence. Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as elaborate hairstyles, gold jewellery or fine clothes. Instead, it should be the beauty of your inner self, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is of great worth in God’s sight.

For worship. Ask God to make you beautiful on the inside: gentle, quiet, at rest in him.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.

For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves. Key words. “Holy women”: the godly women of the Old Testament, like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah, Hannah, Ruth. “Hoped in God”: their hope was not in their husbands or beauty but in God. This gave them security to submit.

By submitting to their own husbands. Key words. Their adornment was a godly submission flowing from hope in God.

As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. Key words. “Lord” (kyrion, master, sir): a respectful form of address in that culture. In Genesis 18:12, Sarah privately referred to Abraham as “my lord.” Even in her inner thoughts, she showed respect. Sarah was not a doormat: she was strong-willed and spoke frankly (Genesis 16:5; 21:10), and God told Abraham to listen to her (Genesis 21:12).

And you are her children. Key words. “Children” (tekna, daughters). As believers are Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7), Christian women become Sarah’s daughters by following her example of faith.

If you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening. Key words. “Do good” (agathopoiousai). “Fear” (phoboumenai, be afraid). “Frightening” (ptoēsin, terror, intimidation, alarm). Christian wives with pagan husbands faced real threats. Submission is not fear-driven. A woman who trusts God need not be terrified by anything, including her husband’s anger (Proverbs 3:25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean wives must use the word “lord” for their husbands today. The principle is respect, not a particular form of words. Nor does it mean Sarah was perfect; she also laughed in unbelief and mistreated Hagar.

In a sentence. This is how the holy women of the past who put their hope in God used to make themselves beautiful: by following their own husbands’ lead, like Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him her lord. You are her daughters if you do what is right and do not give way to fear.

On a Tuesday. What fear is controlling you? Bring it to God, put your hope in him, and do what is right.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.

Likewise, husbands. Key words. “Likewise” (homoiōs): husbands too have duties, though Peter gives them one verse to the wives’ six, perhaps because most husbands in his readership were believers, or because Christian husbands were less common.

Live with your wives in an understanding way. Key words. “Live with” (synoikountes, dwell together, share a home, including the sexual relationship). “In an understanding way” (kata gnōsin, according to knowledge). Husbands must study their wives: know them, understand their needs, feelings and concerns, and live considerately.

Showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel. Key words. “Showing honor” (aponemontes timēn, assigning honour, paying respect). “Weaker vessel” (asthenesterō skeuei, weaker container). “Vessel” is used of both men and women as God’s containers (2 Timothy 2:21). “Weaker” most likely refers to physical strength, and perhaps social vulnerability, in a world where women had few rights. Not weaker morally, intellectually or spiritually. The point is that husbands must not exploit their greater strength, but use it to protect and honour, as one handles fine china with care.

Since they are heirs with you of the grace of life. Key words. “Heirs with you” (synklēronomois, co-heirs, joint heirs). Spiritually, husband and wife are completely equal before God, inheriting the same eternal life (Galatians 3:28). Distinction of roles does not mean distinction of worth.

So that your prayers may not be hindered. Key words. “Hindered” (enkoptesthai, cut in on, blocked, obstructed). A husband who mistreats his wife will find his prayers blocked. God takes the treatment of wives very seriously (Malachi 2:13–16). Relationship with God and relationship with one’s wife are bound together.

What it does not mean. “Weaker vessel” does not mean inferior. Peter immediately calls wives co-heirs. Nor does it give husbands authority to dominate; it requires them to honour.

In a sentence. Husbands, in the same way, be considerate as you live with your wives, and treat them with respect as the physically weaker partner and as co-heirs with you of the gracious gift of life, so that nothing will hinder your prayers.

On a Tuesday. Husbands: what does your wife need from you this week? Ask her, listen, and honour her in a specific way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All of you: be like-minded, sympathetic, loving, tender-hearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, as Psalm 34 teaches: the Lord sees the righteous and hears their prayers. If you suffer for doing right, you are blessed. Do not fear your opponents, but honour Christ as Lord in your hearts, and be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Forgotten Half of Verse 15

Repay evil with blessing. Be ready to give a reason for your hope — with gentleness and respect.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Slandered believers were told to fear the Lord, not their accusers.

Now: A life that raises questions, and answers them courteously, is the best reply to slander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.

Finally, all of you. Key words. “Finally” (to telos, in summary). Now to every believer.

Have unity of mind. Key words. “Unity of mind” (homophrones, like-minded, harmonious). Agreement on what matters most (Philippians 2:2).

Sympathy. Key words. “Sympathy” (sympatheis, feeling with, sharing feelings). Rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep (Romans 12:15).

Brotherly love. Key words. “Brotherly love” (philadelphoi, loving as family).

A tender heart. Key words. “Tender heart” (eusplanchnoi, compassionate, kind-hearted, literally having good inner parts). Deep compassion (Ephesians 4:32).

And a humble mind. Key words. “Humble” (tapeinophrones, lowly-minded). Not thinking too highly of oneself (Philippians 2:3).

Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling. Key words. “Repay” (apodidontes, give back). Do not retaliate in deed or word, as Christ did not (2:23; Romans 12:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:15).

But on the contrary, bless. Key words. “Bless” (eulogountes, speak well of, pray for God’s good). Return blessing for cursing (Luke 6:28; Romans 12:14).

For to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing. Key words. “Called” (eklēthēte), as in 2:21. “Obtain” (klēronomēsēte, inherit). Those who bless will inherit blessing from God. God’s blessing comes to those who bless.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring wrong or never seeking justice. It means personal retaliation is forbidden; we leave vengeance to God and civil authorities (Romans 12:19; 13:4).

In a sentence. Finally, all of you, be like-minded, be sympathetic, love one another as family, be compassionate and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult. On the contrary, repay evil with blessing, because to this you were called, so that you may inherit a blessing.

On a Tuesday. Who has wronged or insulted you recently? Bless them this week: pray for them and speak well of them.

verseByVerse.quote: For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

For Whoever desires to love life and see good days. Key words. From Psalm 34:12–16, the same psalm quoted in 2:3. David wrote it after escaping from danger by pretending to be mad (Psalm 34 title; 1 Samuel 21:10–15). A psalm of God’s protection of the persecuted righteous. “Love life” and “good days”: a blessed life, now and forever.

Let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Key words. First, control your speech: no reviling (v. 9), no lies.

Let him turn away from evil and do good. Key words. Second, actively turn from evil and pursue good.

Let him seek peace and pursue it. Key words. Third, peace: not passively waiting for it, but chasing it (Romans 12:18; Hebrews 12:14).

For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. Key words. God watches over the righteous with care, and hears their prayers. The persecuted are not forgotten.

But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. Key words. God opposes evildoers. Peter stops the quotation before the psalm’s next line (“to cut off the memory of them from the earth”), perhaps leaving room for persecutors to repent.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that the righteous will never suffer. The next verses deal with suffering for righteousness. It means God sees, hears and cares, and that ultimately the righteous will see good days.

In a sentence. For, “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep their tongue from evil and their lips from deceitful speech. They must turn from evil and do good; they must seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears are attentive to their prayer, but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.”

For worship. Thank God that his eyes are on you and his ears open to your prayers. Bring him your troubles today.

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,

Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? Key words. “Harm” (kakōsōn, do evil to, injure). “Zealous” (zēlōtai, eager, passionate). Generally, people who do good are not attacked. And ultimately no one can harm the believer’s soul (Matthew 10:28; Romans 8:31).

But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed. Key words. “Even if” (ei kai, but if indeed): the Greek form suggests a real but not constant possibility. “For righteousness’ sake” (dia dikaiosynēn): because of doing right, because of loyalty to Christ. “Blessed” (makarioi): echoing Jesus’ beatitude (Matthew 5:10–12). Suffering for Christ is not a curse but a blessing.

Have no fear of them, nor be troubled. Key words. From Isaiah 8:12. “Fear of them” (ton phobon autōn, their fear, what they fear, or fear of them). “Troubled” (tarachthēte, shaken, agitated, disturbed). In Isaiah, God told the prophet not to fear what the people feared (the Assyrian threat), but to fear God alone (Isaiah 8:13). Peter applies it: do not be intimidated by persecutors.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never feel fear. It means fear does not govern them. They honour Christ above their fear (v. 15).

In a sentence. Who is going to harm you if you are eager to do good? But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. Do not fear their threats; do not be frightened.

On a Tuesday. What are you afraid of losing if you stand for Christ? Bring that fear to him and choose to honour him above it.

verseByVerse.quote: but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,
verseByVerse.commentary:
but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,

But in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy. Key words. From Isaiah 8:13: “But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear.” In Isaiah, “the LORD” is Yahweh. Peter applies the verse directly to Christ: Christ is the LORD. A strong statement of his deity. “Honor as holy” (hagiasate, sanctify, set apart, revere). Enthrone Christ in your heart as Lord. Fear of Christ displaces fear of people.

Always being prepared to make a defense. Key words. “Prepared” (hetoimoi, ready). “Defense” (apologian, a reasoned answer, a legal defence in court; from which comes “apologetics”). Christians should be able to explain why they believe, whether in a courtroom or a conversation.

To anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you. Key words. “Asks” (aitounti, demands, requests). “Reason” (logon, account, explanation). “Hope”: the living hope of 1:3. Christian hope in suffering is so striking that people will ask about it.

Yet do it with gentleness and respect. Key words. “Gentleness” (prautētos, meekness), toward the person asking. “Respect” (phobou, fear, reverence), perhaps reverence toward God, or respect toward the questioner. Not arrogant, combative or contemptuous. How we answer matters as much as what we say.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must be a trained philosopher. It means every Christian should know the gospel and why they believe it well enough to explain it simply, and be ready to do so.

In a sentence. But in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you to explain the hope you have. But do it with gentleness and respect,

On a Tuesday. Could you explain your hope in Christ in two minutes? Practise it this week, and pray for an opportunity to share it.

verseByVerse.quote: having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil.

Having a good conscience. Key words. “Good conscience” (syneidēsin agathēn): a conscience that does not accuse, because one has lived rightly (Acts 23:1; 1 Timothy 1:5, 19). Not sinlessness, but integrity.

So that, when you are slandered. Key words. “Slandered” (katalaleisthe, spoken against), as in 2:12.

Those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. Key words. “Revile” (epēreazontes, insult, mistreat, abuse). “Good behavior in Christ” (agathēn en Christō anastrophēn): good conduct flowing from union with Christ. “Put to shame” (kataischynthōsin, be embarrassed, exposed as wrong). When the accusations are obviously false, the accusers are shamed.

For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God’s will, than for doing evil. Key words. “If that should be God’s will” (ei theloi to thelēma tou theou): suffering comes only within God’s will (4:19). He is sovereign over it. If we must suffer, let it be for doing good, not for wrongdoing (2:20; 4:15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God delights in our suffering. It means he permits and uses it for good, and that suffering for righteousness is honourable, while suffering for sin is not.

In a sentence. keeping a clear conscience, so that those who speak maliciously against your good behaviour in Christ may be ashamed of their slander. For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.

For worship. Ask God to keep your conscience clear, so that if you suffer, it will be for doing good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Christ's Suffering and Cosmic Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter grounds his call to suffer well in Christ’s own suffering. Christ died once for all for sins, the innocent for the guilty, to bring us to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive by the Spirit, and in that state he went and made a proclamation to the imprisoned spirits who had disobeyed long ago in Noah’s day, while God waited patiently as the ark was built and a few people, eight in all, were brought safely through the water. That water foreshadows baptism, which saves now, not by washing dirt from the body, but as a pledge or appeal to God from a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. He has gone into heaven and is at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities and powers made subject to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ’s Victory

Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. Verses 19–20 are disputed, but no reading offers a second chance after death.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Noah's household of eight was a small minority brought safely through.

Now: Every power believers fear has already been made subject to the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,

For Christ also suffered once for sins. Key words. “Also”: Christ is the supreme example of suffering for doing good. “Once” (hapax, once for all), as in Hebrews 9:26–28. His suffering was unique and complete. “For sins” (peri hamartiōn): the phrase used in the Greek Old Testament for the sin offering. His death was a sacrifice for sin.

The righteous for the unrighteous. Key words. “Righteous” (dikaios): Christ, the sinless one (Acts 3:14). “For” (hyper, on behalf of, in place of). “Unrighteous” (adikōn): us, sinners. This is substitution: the innocent dying in place of the guilty (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:6–8). Penal substitution in a single phrase.

That he might bring us to God. Key words. “Bring” (prosagagē, lead to, usher into the presence of, as a courtier introduces someone to the king). The goal of the atonement: access to God, reconciliation, fellowship (Ephesians 2:18; 3:12).

Being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. Key words. “Put to death in the flesh” (thanatōtheis sarki): he truly died, physically, in his human body. “Made alive in the spirit” (zōopoiētheis pneumati): either “in the Spirit” (by the Holy Spirit, who raised him, Romans 8:11) or “in the spiritual realm” (in the realm of the Spirit, his resurrection life). The contrast is between the sphere of the flesh (earthly, mortal existence) and the sphere of the Spirit (resurrection life, the new creation). It refers to his resurrection, in which he was raised in a glorified body empowered by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45; Romans 1:4; 1 Timothy 3:16).

What it does not mean. “Made alive in the spirit” does not mean Jesus’ body stayed dead and only his spirit lived on. He rose bodily (Luke 24:39). Nor does it mean his human spirit died; at death, his spirit went to the Father (Luke 23:46).

In a sentence. For Christ also suffered once for all for sins, the righteous one for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive by the Spirit.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he, the righteous one, died for you, the unrighteous, to bring you to God. Come to God through him now.

verseByVerse.quote: in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison, because they formerly did not obey, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.

In which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison. Key words. One of the hardest passages in the New Testament. Main views: (1) Between his death and resurrection, Christ went to the realm of the dead and preached the gospel to the souls of those who died in Noah’s flood, giving them a second chance. (2) Between his death and resurrection, Christ descended to the place of the dead and announced his victory to the dead, without offering a second chance. (3) After his resurrection, in his ascension, Christ proclaimed his victory to fallen angels (spirits) imprisoned for their sin in Noah’s day (2 Peter 2:4–5; Jude 6; Genesis 6:1–4). (4) Christ, by the Spirit, preached through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who rejected the message and are now spirits in prison (in hell). “In which” (en hō): in the Spirit, or in the spiritual realm. “Proclaimed” (ekēryxen, heralded, announced): not necessarily the gospel; a herald may announce victory or judgement. “Spirits” (pneumasin): in the New Testament, used alone, this word usually means angelic beings, not human souls (Hebrews 1:14; Matthew 8:16). “In prison” (en phylakē, under guard).

Because they formerly did not obey, when God’s patience waited in the days of Noah. Key words. “Did not obey” (apeithēsasin, disobeyed). “God’s patience waited” (apexedecheto hē tou theou makrothymia): God waited, perhaps 120 years (Genesis 6:3), while Noah built and preached (2 Peter 2:5, “a herald of righteousness”).

While the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water. Key words. Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives (Genesis 7:13). “Brought safely through” (diesōthēsan, were saved through). The water that destroyed the world carried the ark to safety. A small minority was saved, as Peter’s readers were a small, persecuted minority.

Where Christians differ: did Christ offer the dead a second chance? Verdict: The view that Christ offered salvation to the dead contradicts Scripture’s clear teaching that destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27), and it would be strange to offer it only to Noah’s generation. The two strongest views are the third (Christ, in his resurrection and ascension, proclaimed his triumph over the fallen angels imprisoned since Noah’s day, as 2 Peter 2:4–5 and Jude 6 describe) and the fourth (Christ by his Spirit preached through Noah to those who are now in prison). The third fits the word “spirits,” the link with verse 22 (angels subjected to him), and the context of Christ’s victory. Either way, the point is clear: Christ suffered and was vindicated; he triumphed over every evil power; and his people, though few and persecuted like Noah’s family, will be saved. There is no second chance after death, and no purgatory.

What it does not mean. It does not teach that Christ went to hell to suffer further for sins. His suffering was finished on the cross (John 19:30). The phrase “he descended into hell” in the Apostles’ Creed is understood by Reformed churches to mean that he truly died and remained under death’s power for a time, bearing the full weight of God’s wrath on the cross.

In a sentence. After being made alive, he went and made a proclamation to the imprisoned spirits, who had disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In it only a few people, eight in all, were saved through water.

For worship. Praise Christ, who triumphed over every evil power. You, like Noah’s family, are safe in him.
verseByVerse.note: One of the hardest passages in the New Testament. Main views: Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day; or after his death he proclaimed victory to fallen angels imprisoned for the sins of Noah’s time.

verseByVerse.quote: Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.

Baptism, which corresponds to this. Key words. “Corresponds” (antitypon, antitype, counterpart, fulfilment of a pattern). The flood was a type or picture; baptism is its counterpart. As Noah’s family passed through the waters of judgement in the ark and were saved, so believers pass through the waters of baptism in Christ.

Now saves you. Key words. “Saves” (sōzei). A surprising statement, immediately qualified.

Not as a removal of dirt from the body. Key words. Peter immediately explains what he does not mean: the water itself does not save. It is not an external washing that has power in itself.

But as an appeal to God for a good conscience. Key words. “Appeal” (eperōtēma, request, pledge, answer to a question). Either the believer’s appeal to God for a cleansed conscience, or the pledge of a good conscience toward God, the response made at baptism to the question, “Do you believe?” Baptism saves as the outward expression of inward faith, the believer’s commitment to God and request for cleansing, based on Christ’s work.

Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. Key words. The saving power is not in the water but in Christ’s resurrection (1:3). Baptism saves because it unites us symbolically with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4; Colossians 2:12), and faith receives the reality.

Who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God. Key words. His ascension and enthronement (Acts 1:9–11; Hebrews 1:3).

With angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him. Key words. “Subjected” (hypotagentōn, placed under). All spiritual powers, good and evil, are under Christ’s authority (Ephesians 1:20–22; Colossians 2:15). Persecuted believers need not fear; Christ rules over every power behind their persecutors.

Where Christians differ: does baptism itself save? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some others hold that baptism conveys regeneration and forgiveness. Verdict: Peter explicitly denies that the water itself saves (“not as a removal of dirt from the body”). Baptism saves as the appeal or pledge of a good conscience, that is, as the expression of faith, through Christ’s resurrection. The sign is so closely tied to the reality it signifies that Scripture can speak of the sign as doing what the reality does, as when the Lord’s Supper is called “the body of Christ.” Salvation comes through faith in the risen Christ; baptism is the outward sign and seal of that faith, rightly given to those who profess it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism is unimportant or optional. Christ commanded it (Matthew 28:19), and it is the normal public mark of entering his people. But it is not the cause of salvation.

In a sentence. And this water symbolises baptism, which now saves you also, not by washing dirt from the body, but as the pledge of a clear conscience toward God. It saves you by the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who has gone into heaven and is at God’s right hand, with angels, authorities and powers placed under him.

For worship. Remember your baptism with thankfulness: not the water, but the risen Christ to whom it united you, who reigns over every power.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Likewise, wives, be subject to your own husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives,<sup>2</sup>when they see your respectful and pure conduct.<sup>3</sup>Do not let your adorning be external—the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear—<sup>4</sup>but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious.<sup>5</sup>For this is how the holy women who hoped in God used to adorn themselves, by submitting to their own husbands,<sup>6</sup>as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. And you are her children, if you do good and do not fear anything that is frightening.<sup>7</sup>Likewise, husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor to the woman as the weaker vessel, since they are heirs with you of the grace of life, so that your prayers may not be hindered.<sup>8</sup>Finally, all of you, have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart, and a humble mind.<sup>9</sup>Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary, bless, for to this you were called, that you may obtain a blessing.<sup>10</sup>For "Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit;<sup>11</sup>let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it.<sup>12</sup>For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil."<sup>13</sup>Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good?<sup>14</sup>But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed.
