Have no fear of them, nor be troubled,<sup>15</sup>but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect,<sup>16</sup>having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame.<sup>17</sup>For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil.<sup>18</sup>For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit,<sup>19</sup>in which he went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison,<sup>20</sup>because they formerly did not obey, when God's patience waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being prepared, in which a few, that is, eight persons, were brought safely through water.<sup>21</sup>Baptism, which corresponds to this, now saves you, not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,<sup>22</sup>who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.

4.title: Stewards of Grace: The Meaning of Suffering
4.overview: Chapter 4 returns to suffering in the light of the end: “The end of all things is at hand” (v. 7). The first half (vv. 1–11) shows how suffering settles a believer’s break with the old life, and how a church facing the end should live: clear-headed for prayer, loving earnestly, hospitable, and using every gift for others. The second half (vv. 12–19) speaks directly to the fiery trial: do not be surprised; rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings; do not be ashamed to suffer as a Christian; and entrust your soul to a faithful Creator.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Stewards of God's Varied Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since Christ suffered, arm yourselves with the same mind: suffering for him settles our break with sin. You have spent enough time living as pagans do; your old friends are puzzled and slander you, but they will answer to God. The end is near, so be clear-headed for prayer, love one another deeply, show hospitality without grumbling, and use each gift to serve others, so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Stewards of God's Varied Grace

Suffering for Christ settles a believer's break with sin. Because the end is near, stay clear-headed for prayer, love earnestly, and use each gift to serve others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Neighbours were baffled when converts no longer joined them, and spoke against them.

Now: Love covers a multitude of sins: it does not pass offences around.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin, so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.

Meaning first. 1 Peter 4 prepares believers to live for God in a world that will mock and persecute them. Christ suffered in the flesh; so they must arm themselves with the same mindset, finished with living for sinful desires and now living for God’s will (vv. 1–2). Their former pagan life of indulgence is over; former friends are surprised and slander them, but those friends will give account to the Judge of the living and the dead, which is why the gospel was preached to believers who have since died, so that though condemned by people they live with God (vv. 3–6). Because the end is near, they should pray with clear minds, love one another deeply, since love covers many sins, show hospitality without grumbling, and use every gift as faithful stewards of God’s grace, speaking God’s words and serving in God’s strength, so that God is glorified through Christ (vv. 7–11). They should not be surprised at the fiery trial, but rejoice as they share Christ’s sufferings, knowing they will rejoice even more when his glory is revealed; if insulted for Christ’s name, they are blessed, for the Spirit of glory rests on them (vv. 12–14). They must not suffer as wrongdoers, but if they suffer as Christians, they should not be ashamed but glorify God (vv. 15–16). Judgement begins with God’s household; if the righteous are saved only with difficulty, how terrible will be the end of the ungodly. So those who suffer by God’s will should entrust themselves to their faithful Creator and keep doing good (vv. 17–19).

Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh. Key words. “Therefore”: picking up 3:18. “In the flesh” (sarki): in his body, physically, to death.

Arm yourselves with the same way of thinking. Key words. “Arm yourselves” (hoplisasthe, put on armour, equip yourselves as soldiers). “Way of thinking” (ennoian, mindset, attitude, resolve). Christ’s attitude was willingness to suffer rather than sin, and to do God’s will at any cost. The Christian life is warfare, and the right mindset is armour.

For whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin. Key words. A difficult phrase. Most likely: the person who has made a decisive break with sin, embracing suffering for Christ rather than compromise, has thereby shown that sin no longer rules him (Romans 6:7). Suffering for doing right proves that one has chosen God over sin. It may also allude to union with Christ’s death: having died with him, we are finished with sin as a master.

So as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God. Key words. “Rest of the time”: the remainder of earthly life. “Human passions” (anthrōpōn epithymiais, the desires of people). “Will of God” (thelēmati theou). The great reorientation: from living for desires to living for God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering makes us sinless or that physical suffering itself removes sin. Only Christ’s suffering atones. It means willingness to suffer for righteousness shows that sin’s dominion is broken.

In a sentence. Therefore, since Christ suffered in his body, arm yourselves also with the same attitude, because whoever suffers in the body is done with sin. As a result, they do not live the rest of their earthly lives for evil human desires, but for the will of God.

On a Tuesday. What would it look like to “arm yourself” with Christ’s mindset this week, choosing God’s will even when it costs you?

verseByVerse.quote: For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;

For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do. Key words. “Suffices” (arketos, is enough). With a touch of irony: you have had more than enough time for that. “Gentiles”: pagans, unbelievers (2:12). Peter’s readers were mostly former pagans.

Living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry. Key words. Six marks of pagan life. “Sensuality” (aselgeiais, unrestrained immorality, shameless excess). “Passions” (epithymiais, lusts). “Drunkenness” (oinophlygiais, overflowing with wine). “Orgies” (kōmois, carousing, wild revelry, drunken processions in the streets, often linked to the cult of Dionysus). “Drinking parties” (potois, drinking bouts). “Lawless idolatry” (athemitois eidōlolatriais, abominable, forbidden idolatry). Much of this was connected to pagan religious festivals and trade guild banquets held in temples.

With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them. Key words. “Surprised” (xenizontai, think it strange, are astonished). Former friends could not understand why converts no longer joined in. Christians were seen as antisocial, odd, and disloyal to civic religion.

In the same flood of debauchery. Key words. “Join” (syntrechontōn, run together with, rush along with). “Flood” (anachysin, pouring out, overflow, outpouring, like a sewer flowing over). “Debauchery” (asōtias, wild living, dissipation), the word used of the prodigal son (Luke 15:13). A vivid picture: a crowd rushing headlong into a torrent of excess.

And they malign you. Key words. “Malign” (blasphēmountes, slander, abuse, speak evil of). They mocked and slandered the Christians, perhaps as killjoys, haters of humanity, or atheists.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be joyless or avoid all social occasions. Jesus attended feasts (John 2:1–11). It means they must not join in sinful excess.

In a sentence. For you have spent enough time in the past doing what pagans choose to do: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, wild partying, drinking bouts and detestable idolatry. They are surprised that you no longer join them in their reckless, wild living, and they heap abuse on you.

On a Tuesday. Are you being mocked for not joining in something sinful? Take heart; that is exactly what Peter’s readers faced. Stand firm.

verseByVerse.quote: but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.

But they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. Key words. “Give account” (apodōsousin logon, render an account). The slanderers will answer to God. “Ready” (hetoimōs, prepared, about to). “Judge the living and the dead”: Christ, or God the Father (Acts 10:42; 2 Timothy 4:1). All people, whether alive at his return or already dead, will be judged.

For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead. Key words. Another difficult verse. “Those who are dead” (nekrois). Most likely, believers who heard the gospel while alive and have since died, perhaps through martyrdom or natural death. Some in the churches may have worried: what good did the gospel do for those believers who died? Peter answers: the gospel was preached to them in life so that, although they died (“judged in the flesh,” suffering death like all people, or condemned by human judges), they now live with God in the spirit.

That though judged in the flesh the way people are. Key words. “Judged in the flesh” (krithōsi sarki): they suffered physical death, the common human judgement for sin (Romans 5:12), or they were condemned by human courts. “The way people are” (kata anthrōpous, according to human standards).

They might live in the spirit the way God does. Key words. “Live in the spirit” (zōsi pneumati): they are alive in God’s presence, in the spiritual realm, awaiting the resurrection (Hebrews 12:23; Revelation 6:9–11). “The way God does” (kata theon, according to God, in God’s estimation). Human verdict: condemned and dead. God’s verdict: alive.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a second chance after death? Some read this verse, alongside 3:19, as teaching that the gospel is preached to the dead in the afterlife, giving them an opportunity to believe. Verdict: The verb is past tense (“was preached”), and the most natural reading is that the gospel was preached to people while they were alive, who are now dead. Scripture consistently teaches that death fixes one’s destiny (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no second chance after death. The verse comforts believers: those who died in Christ are not lost but live with God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the departed believers are unconscious or in purgatory. They are alive with God, consciously enjoying his presence.

In a sentence. But they will have to give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead. For this is the reason the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that, though judged in the body by human standards, they might live in the spirit by God’s standard.

For worship. Thank God for believers you have known who have died. They are alive with him now, and you will see them again.

verseByVerse.quote: The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.

The end of all things is at hand. Key words. “End” (telos, goal, completion, conclusion). “All things”: the present age, history itself. “At hand” (ēngiken, has drawn near), as in James 5:8. The death and resurrection of Christ have brought the end near. The next great event in God’s plan is Christ’s return, which could come at any time.

Therefore be self-controlled. Key words. “Self-controlled” (sōphronēsate, be sensible, of sound mind). Not panicked or carried away by end-time speculation, but clear-headed.

And sober-minded. Key words. “Sober-minded” (nēpsate, be alert, clear-headed, free from intoxication), as in 1:13 and 5:8. The opposite of the drunkenness of verse 3.

For the sake of your prayers. Key words. Literally “for prayers.” The purpose of a clear mind is prayer. Spiritual alertness enables effective prayer. Jesus told his disciples to watch and pray (Mark 14:38), as Peter had failed to do in Gethsemane.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should sell everything, stop working and wait on a hilltop. Nearness of the end calls for clear thinking, prayer, love and service (vv. 8–11), not frenzy. Nor does it mean Peter was mistaken; “near” describes the nature of the whole age (2 Peter 3:8–9).

In a sentence. The end of all things is near. Therefore be alert and of sober mind so that you may pray.

On a Tuesday. Since the end is near, clear your mind of distractions this week, and give yourself to prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.

Above all, keep loving one another earnestly. Key words. “Above all” (pro pantōn, before everything). Love is the top priority. “Earnestly” (ektenē, fervent, stretched out, intense), as in 1:22. Under persecution, the church must hold together in strong love.

Since love covers a multitude of sins. Key words. From Proverbs 10:12 (“love covers all offenses”), as in James 5:20. “Covers” (kalyptei, hides, overlooks). Love does not publicise, exaggerate or hold onto others’ faults, but forgives and overlooks offences (1 Corinthians 13:5, 7). In a church under pressure, members will irritate one another; love covers it.

Show hospitality to one another without grumbling. Key words. “Hospitality” (philoxenoi, love of strangers). Travelling believers and missionaries depended on hospitality, and churches met in homes. “Without grumbling” (aneu gongysmou, without complaining). Hospitality can be tiring and costly; it is to be given cheerfully (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2).

What it does not mean. “Love covers sins” does not mean love earns forgiveness from God, or that love ignores serious sin that needs discipline (Matthew 18:15–17). It means love does not keep a record of wrongs and readily forgives.

In a sentence. Above all, love each other deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. Offer hospitality to one another without grumbling.

On a Tuesday. Is there an offence you are holding onto? Let love cover it. And invite someone for a meal this week, cheerfully.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God’s varied grace: whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

As each has received a gift. Key words. “Each” (hekastos): every believer has at least one gift. “Gift” (charisma, grace-gift), as in Romans 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 12:4. Given by God’s grace, not earned.

Use it to serve one another. Key words. “Serve” (diakonountes, minister). Gifts are for others, not for self-display.

As good stewards of God’s varied grace. Key words. “Stewards” (oikonomoi, household managers), as in Titus 1:7. We do not own our gifts; we manage them for God. “Varied” (poikilēs, many-coloured), the same word as “various trials” (1:6). God’s grace is as multi-coloured as our trials.

Whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God. Key words. Two broad categories of gifts: speaking and serving. “Oracles” (logia, words, utterances of God). Those who teach or preach must speak as if delivering God’s own message, faithfully conveying his word, not their own opinions (2 Timothy 4:2).

Whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies. Key words. “Supplies” (chorēgei, provides abundantly; originally used of someone who paid for a chorus in Greek drama, providing generously). Practical service depends on God’s strength, not ours.

In order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. Key words. The purpose of all gifts: God’s glory, through Christ.

To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. Key words. A doxology. “Him”: God, or Christ. Either way, all glory is his.

What it does not mean. “Speaks oracles of God” does not mean preachers today receive new revelation. It means they must speak faithfully what God has already said in Scripture, with the seriousness that befits God’s word. The apostolic gifts of revelation belonged to the foundational era; today God speaks through his completed word.

In a sentence. Each of you should use whatever gift you have received to serve others, as faithful stewards of God’s grace in its many forms. If anyone speaks, they should do so as one who speaks the very words of God. If anyone serves, they should do so with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be praised through Jesus Christ. To him be the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.

On a Tuesday. What gift has God given you? Use it this week to serve someone in your church, in his strength and for his glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not be surprised by the fiery trial, as though something strange were happening. Rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings. If you are insulted for his name, the Spirit of glory rests on you. Do not suffer as a wrongdoer or a meddler; but if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed. Judgment begins with God’s household. So those who suffer by God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and keep doing good.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgement Beginning at Home

Do not be surprised by the fiery trial. To suffer as a Christian is no shame; entrust your soul to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: “Christian” was probably an outsiders’ insult, and Peter told them to wear it.

Now: Make sure any suffering is for Christ’s name, not for wrongdoing or interfering.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.

Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial. Key words. “Surprised” (xenizesthe, think it strange), the same word used of the pagans (v. 4). They think it strange that you do not join them; you should not think it strange that they persecute you. “Fiery trial” (pyrōsei, burning, refining fire). Severe persecution. Some think this anticipates Nero’s persecution (AD 64), in which Christians were burned as torches.

When it comes upon you to test you. Key words. “Test” (peirasmon, trial). God uses the fire to refine faith (1:6–7).

As though something strange were happening to you. Key words. Suffering for Christ is normal, not abnormal (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12).

But rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings. Key words. “Share” (koinōneite, participate in, have fellowship in). Suffering for Christ is fellowship with him (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24). Not adding to his atonement, which is complete, but sharing in the opposition the world gave him.

That you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed. Key words. “Be glad” (agalliōmenoi, exult, be overjoyed). Present joy in suffering leads to overflowing joy at his return. The pattern: suffering, then glory (1:11; Romans 8:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should enjoy pain itself. They rejoice in what the suffering means and leads to.

In a sentence. Dear friends, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that has come on you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed when his glory is revealed.

For worship. If you are suffering for Christ, thank him that you are sharing in his sufferings, and look forward to sharing his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.

If you are insulted for the name of Christ. Key words. “Insulted” (oneidizesthe, reproached, reviled). “For the name of Christ”: because you bear his name and belong to him. Persecution was often verbal: mockery, slander, exclusion.

You are blessed. Key words. “Blessed” (makarioi), echoing Jesus (Matthew 5:11–12).

Because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you. Key words. “The Spirit of glory and of God”: the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s glory. “Rests upon you” (anapauetai, rests, abides), echoing Isaiah 11:2, where the Spirit rests on the Messiah. As the glory cloud rested on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35), so the Spirit rests on persecuted believers. Their insults are a sign that God’s glory is with them. Like Stephen, whose face shone like an angel as he was attacked (Acts 6:15; 7:55).

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add, “On their part he is blasphemed, but on your part he is glorified.” The earliest manuscripts lack it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only persecuted believers have the Spirit. All believers have him (Romans 8:9). It means that in persecution the Spirit’s presence is specially manifest and real.

In a sentence. If you are insulted because of the name of Christ, you are blessed, for the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.

For worship. If you are mocked for Christ, take heart: God’s glory rests on you. Thank him for his Spirit’s presence.

verseByVerse.quote: But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler. Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.

But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer. Key words. Suffering is only blessed if it is undeserved. “Evildoer” (kakopoios, criminal, wrongdoer).

Or as a meddler. Key words. “Meddler” (allotriepiskopos, one who oversees others’ affairs, a busybody). A rare word, perhaps coined by Peter. Perhaps Christians who stirred up trouble by interfering, tactlessly condemning pagan customs, or causing unnecessary offence. Surprising to see it in a list with murder, but it shows that Christians can bring suffering on themselves by foolishness.

Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian. Key words. “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28). It meant “Christ’s people” or “partisan of Christ,” perhaps used mockingly. Here it appears to be becoming a legal charge.

Let him not be ashamed. Key words. “Ashamed” (aischynesthō). There is no shame in suffering for Christ (Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8, 12).

But let him glorify God in that name. Key words. “In that name” (en tō onomati toutō): because he bears the name “Christian.” What was intended as an insult becomes a badge of honour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian who suffers is suffering for Christ. Sometimes we suffer for our own folly or sin. We must examine ourselves honestly.

In a sentence. If you suffer, it should not be as a murderer or thief or any other kind of criminal, or even as a meddler. However, if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but praise God that you bear that name.

On a Tuesday. If you face criticism this week, ask honestly: is this for Christ, or for my own fault? If for Christ, wear the name with joy.
verseByVerse.note: “Christian” was first a nickname given by outsiders; it appears only three times in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?" Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And “If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” Therefore let those who suffer according to God’s will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.

For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God. Key words. “Time” (kairos, the appointed season). “Judgment” (krima). “Household of God” (oikou tou theou): the church, God’s temple and family (2:5; 1 Timothy 3:15). Echoing Ezekiel 9:6, where God’s judgement begins at his sanctuary, and Malachi 3:1–5, where the Lord refines the temple. For believers, the “judgement” is the refining fire of suffering, purifying them (vv. 12, 17).

And if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God? Key words. “Outcome” (telos, end). If God’s refining is this painful for his own children, how terrible will his final judgement be for those who reject the gospel (2 Thessalonians 1:8–9).

And If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner? Key words. From Proverbs 11:31 (Greek). “Scarcely” (molis, with difficulty). Not that salvation is uncertain or only barely achieved, but that it comes through great difficulty, trial and suffering (Acts 14:22). Salvation is entirely secure because God guards us (1:5), but the road is hard. If the righteous pass through such fire, what of the ungodly?

Therefore let those who suffer according to God’s will. Key words. “According to God’s will” (kata to thelēma tou theou): suffering is not outside God’s control (3:17).

Entrust their souls to a faithful Creator. Key words. “Entrust” (paratithesthōsan, commit, deposit for safekeeping), the word Jesus used on the cross: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (Luke 23:46), echoing Psalm 31:5. “Faithful Creator” (pistō ktistē): the only place in the New Testament God is called “Creator” with this word. The God who made you is faithful; he will care for what he made.

While doing good. Key words. “Doing good” (en agathopoiia). Trusting God does not mean passive resignation. Keep doing good, even while suffering.

What it does not mean. “Scarcely saved” does not mean believers may not make it. Peter has already said they are guarded by God’s power (1:5). It means salvation comes through great tribulation, not ease. And judgement “beginning at the household of God” is fatherly discipline, not condemnation (Hebrews 12:5–11; 1 Corinthians 11:32).

In a sentence. For it is time for judgement to begin with God’s household; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who do not obey the gospel of God? And, “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should commit themselves to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.

For worship. Pray Jesus’ words today: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.” Entrust yourself to your faithful Creator, and keep doing good.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, for whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sin,<sup>2</sup>so as to live for the rest of the time in the flesh no longer for human passions but for the will of God.<sup>3</sup>For the time that is past suffices for doing what the Gentiles want to do, living in sensuality, passions, drunkenness, orgies, drinking parties, and lawless idolatry.<sup>4</sup>With respect to this they are surprised when you do not join them in the same flood of debauchery, and they malign you;<sup>5</sup>but they will give account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.<sup>6</sup>For this is why the gospel was preached even to those who are dead, that though judged in the flesh the way people are, they might live in the spirit the way God does.<sup>7</sup>The end of all things is at hand; therefore be self-controlled and sober-minded for the sake of your prayers.<sup>8</sup>Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins.<sup>9</sup>Show hospitality to one another without grumbling.<sup>10</sup>As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace:<sup>11</sup>whoever speaks, as one who speaks oracles of God; whoever serves, as one who serves by the strength that God supplies—in order that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.<sup>12</sup>Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you.<sup>13</sup>But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed.<sup>14</sup>If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you.<sup>15</sup>But let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler.<sup>16</sup>Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in that name.<sup>17</sup>For it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God; and if it begins with us, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel of God?<sup>18</sup>And "If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?"<sup>19</sup>Therefore let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.

5.title: Humble Yourselves: Elders, Community, and the God of All Grace
5.overview: The last chapter has three movements: elders are to shepherd God’s flock (vv. 1–5); the whole church is to humble itself under God’s mighty hand, cast its anxieties on him and resist the devil (vv. 6–11); and closing greetings place the letter in “Babylon”, almost certainly Rome (vv. 12–14). Its climax is one of the finest benedictions in the New Testament: after a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Shepherd the Flock of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to the elders as a fellow elder. Shepherd God’s flock willingly, not under compulsion; eagerly, not for money; by example, not by domineering. When the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive an unfading crown of glory. Younger people should submit to the elders, and everyone should put on humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Temptations and Their Remedies

Elders are to shepherd God's flock willingly, eagerly and by example — not under compulsion, not for gain, not by domineering. The chief Shepherd is coming.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote to elders as a fellow elder, not as an apostle.

Now: Everyone is to tie on the servant’s apron of humility.

verseByVerse.quote: So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, as well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed:

Meaning first. 1 Peter 5 brings the letter to a close with instructions for a suffering church. Peter, writing as a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings, urges the elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, eagerly and by example, not for money or by domineering, knowing that the Chief Shepherd will give them an unfading crown of glory (vv. 1–4). Younger people should submit to the elders, and everyone should clothe themselves with humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (v. 5). So humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand, casting all your anxieties on him because he cares for you (vv. 6–7). Be alert, because the devil prowls like a roaring lion; resist him, firm in faith, knowing fellow believers worldwide suffer the same (vv. 8–9). After a little suffering, the God of all grace will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (vv. 10–11). The letter ends with a summary (this is the true grace of God; stand firm in it), greetings from “Babylon” and Mark, and a final word of peace (vv. 12–14).

So I exhort the elders among you. Key words. “So” (oun, therefore): because judgement begins at God’s household (4:17), its leaders must be faithful. “Exhort” (parakalō, appeal, urge). “Elders” (presbyterous, plural): the leaders of each local church, also called overseers and shepherds (vv. 2–4; Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7).

As a fellow elder. Key words. “Fellow elder” (sympresbyteros, co-elder, a word perhaps coined by Peter). Remarkable humility. Peter, the leading apostle, does not claim supremacy but stands alongside the elders as one of them.

And a witness of the sufferings of Christ. Key words. “Witness” (martys, eyewitness, one who testifies). Peter saw Jesus’ suffering firsthand: in Gethsemane, at the trial, perhaps at the cross. He also bore witness to it in preaching and by his own suffering.

As well as a partaker in the glory that is going to be revealed. Key words. “Partaker” (koinōnos, sharer). Peter had seen a preview of Christ’s glory at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8; 2 Peter 1:16–18), and he will share it fully at Christ’s return (4:13).

Where Christians differ: was Peter the first pope? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Christ made Peter head of the universal church, with authority passed to the bishops of Rome as his successors. Verdict: Peter calls himself a fellow elder, not a supreme pontiff. Christ is the Chief Shepherd (v. 4), the cornerstone (2:6), and the head of the church (Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18). Peter was a leading apostle and the first to preach to Jews and Gentiles (Acts 2; 10), but the foundation of the church is the apostles and prophets together, with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), and Paul could rebuke Peter publicly (Galatians 2:11–14). The New Testament knows nothing of a papacy or of Peter’s authority being passed to Roman bishops. Local churches are led by a plurality of elders, under Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Peter’s apostolic authority was the same as an ordinary elder’s. He was an apostle and eyewitness, writing Scripture. But he exercised his authority humbly, as a fellow servant.

In a sentence. To the elders among you, I appeal as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings who also will share in the glory to be revealed:

For worship. Thank God for faithful elders in your church. Pray for them by name today.

verseByVerse.quote: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not for shameful gain, but eagerly; not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock.

Shepherd the flock of God that is among you. Key words. “Shepherd” (poimanate, tend, feed, care for as a shepherd). The command Jesus gave Peter: “Tend my sheep” (John 21:16). Shepherding includes feeding (teaching the word), leading, protecting from wolves, seeking the lost, and caring for the weak (Ezekiel 34:1–16; Acts 20:28). “Flock of God”: not the elders’ flock, but God’s. They are under-shepherds, accountable to him.

Exercising oversight. Key words. “Exercising oversight” (episkopountes, overseeing, watching over), from which comes “bishop.” Elders and overseers are the same office.

Not under compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you. Key words. “Under compulsion” (anankastōs, by constraint, reluctantly, because they must). “Willingly” (hekousiōs, voluntarily, gladly). “As God would have you” (kata theon, according to God). Leadership should come from a willing heart that loves God and his people, not from pressure, guilt or duty alone.

Not for shameful gain, but eagerly. Key words. “Shameful gain” (aischrokerdōs, greedy for dishonest money), as in 1 Timothy 3:3, 8 and Titus 1:7. Elders may be paid (1 Timothy 5:17–18), but money must not be the motive. “Eagerly” (prothymōs, with enthusiasm, readiness, zeal).

Not domineering over those in your charge. Key words. “Domineering” (katakyrieuontes, lording it over, ruling harshly), the word Jesus used of pagan rulers (Mark 10:42). “Those in your charge” (tōn klērōn, the portions, the allotted ones): the people entrusted to them. Leaders must not be bullies or tyrants.

But being examples to the flock. Key words. “Examples” (typoi, patterns, models). Lead by example, not by force (1 Timothy 4:12; Titus 2:7). Shepherds in the ancient Near East walked ahead of their flocks; the sheep followed.

What it does not mean. “Not domineering” does not mean elders have no authority. They lead and must be obeyed (v. 5; Hebrews 13:17). It means their authority is exercised humbly, by example, for the flock’s good.

In a sentence. Be shepherds of God’s flock that is under your care, watching over them, not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing dishonest gain, but eager to serve; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.

On a Tuesday. Whatever leadership you have, in a home, a group or a workplace, lead by example and service this week, not by control.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory.

And when the chief Shepherd appears. Key words. “Chief Shepherd” (archipoimenos, head shepherd): Jesus Christ (2:25; John 10:11; Hebrews 13:20). Elders are under-shepherds; he is the Chief. “Appears” (phanerōthentos, is revealed): at his return.

You will receive the unfading crown of glory. Key words. “Unfading” (amarantinon, made of amaranth, a flower that was thought never to fade), related to the unfading inheritance (1:4). Victory wreaths in the ancient games were made of leaves or flowers that withered within days. “Crown of glory” (stephanon tēs doxēs): the crown that consists of glory. Faithful shepherds may receive little thanks on earth, but Christ will reward them with lasting glory (1 Corinthians 9:25; 2 Timothy 4:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean only elders receive crowns. All believers share in glory. But Christ will specially honour faithful shepherds.

In a sentence. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.

For worship. If you serve faithfully without recognition, look ahead: the Chief Shepherd sees, and he will reward.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another, for “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”

Likewise, you who are younger, be subject to the elders. Key words. “Younger” (neōteroi): younger people in the church, who might be tempted to be impatient or rebellious, or perhaps a group of younger men who served the church practically (Acts 5:6, 10). “Elders” here may mean the office or simply older people; probably the office, continuing from verses 1–4. “Be subject” (hypotagēte), the same word as 2:13, 18; 3:1.

Clothe yourselves, all of you, with humility toward one another. Key words. “All of you”: humility is for everyone, not just the young. “Clothe yourselves” (enkombōsasthe, tie on, put on like an apron). A rare word: the apron slaves tied on to serve. Peter may be remembering Jesus tying a towel around himself to wash the disciples’ feet, including Peter’s (John 13:4–17). Put on humility like a servant’s apron.

For God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Key words. From Proverbs 3:34 (Greek), also quoted in James 4:6. “Opposes” (antitassetai, sets himself in battle against). God resists the proud; he pours grace on the humble.

What it does not mean. It does not mean young people have no voice or gifts. Timothy was young and a leader (1 Timothy 4:12). It means respect for godly leaders, and humility for everyone.

In a sentence. In the same way, you who are younger, submit yourselves to your elders. All of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because, “God opposes the proud but shows favour to the humble.”

On a Tuesday. Tie on the apron of humility this week. Find a way to serve someone, especially someone you might think beneath you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Cast Your Anxieties, and Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter tells his readers to humble themselves under God’s strong hand, so that he will lift them up in due time, and to throw all their worries onto him because he cares for them. They must stay sober and alert, because their enemy the devil prowls like a hungry lion looking for someone to devour; they are to resist him, firm in faith, knowing that believers throughout the world are going through the same sufferings. After they have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called them to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, establish and strengthen them. To him belongs power for ever. Peter adds that he has written briefly through Silvanus to encourage them and testify that this is the true grace of God, and they must stand firm in it. He sends greetings from the church in “Babylon” and from Mark, asks them to greet one another with a kiss of love, and wishes peace to all who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Worry Is Treated as Pride

Humble yourselves by casting all your anxieties on God, because he cares for you. After a little while, the God of all grace will himself restore you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The devil prowled like a roaring lion, looking for anyone cut off from the flock.

Now: Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing the same sufferings are shared by believers throughout the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you.

Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God. Key words. “Humble yourselves” (tapeinōthēte, be humbled, accept humbling). “Mighty hand of God”: the Old Testament image of God’s power in delivering his people from Egypt (Exodus 3:19; 6:1; Deuteronomy 9:26). Also his hand in disciplining them. Accept God’s dealings with you, including suffering, without resentment or resistance. The same hand that humbles also exalts.

So that at the proper time he may exalt you. Key words. “Proper time” (en kairō, in due season): God’s timing, not ours. “Exalt” (hypsōsē, lift up). As he exalted Christ after his humiliation (Philippians 2:8–9; James 4:10).

Casting all your anxieties on him. Key words. “Casting” (epiripsantes, throwing upon, as one throws a garment onto a donkey for it to carry; Luke 19:35). Echoing Psalm 55:22: “Cast your burden on the LORD.” Humbling ourselves includes admitting we cannot carry our worries and throwing them onto God. “All” (pasan): every one, large and small. “Anxieties” (merimnan, cares, worries; the word Jesus used in Matthew 6:25–34). Pride insists on carrying them alone; humility hands them over.

Because he cares for you. Key words. “Cares” (melei, it matters to him, he is concerned). The reason we can cast our worries on him: he cares about us personally. A wordplay: our “anxieties” (merimna) and his “care” (melei). We are not burdening an indifferent God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should never plan or take responsibility. It means we should not be crushed by worry, but trust God with what we cannot control.

In a sentence. Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that he may lift you up in due time. Throw all your worries onto him, because he cares for you.

For worship. Name each of your worries to God today, one by one, and cast them on him. He cares for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.

Be sober-minded; be watchful. Key words. “Sober-minded” (nēpsate, clear-headed), as in 1:13 and 4:7. “Watchful” (grēgorēsate, stay awake, alert). Jesus told Peter in Gethsemane to watch and pray; Peter fell asleep and then denied him (Mark 14:37–38, 66–72). Peter knew the cost of not being watchful.

Your adversary the devil. Key words. “Adversary” (antidikos, opponent in a lawsuit, accuser). “Devil” (diabolos, slanderer). Satan accuses believers before God (Job 1–2; Zechariah 3:1; Revelation 12:10) and slanders them through human persecutors. He is real, personal and hostile.

Prowls around like a roaring lion. Key words. “Prowls” (peripatei, walks about). “Roaring lion”: lions roar to terrify their prey (Psalm 22:13; Ezekiel 22:25). The devil uses fear, persecution and intimidation to make believers flee from faith. Under Nero, Christians were literally thrown to lions.

Seeking someone to devour. Key words. “Devour” (katapiein, swallow up, gulp down). He looks for the isolated, weak or careless.

Resist him, firm in your faith. Key words. “Resist” (antistēte, stand against), as in James 4:7. “Firm” (stereoi, solid, steadfast, like a rock). Peter, the “rock,” urges firmness. Resistance comes through faith: trusting God and his word (Ephesians 6:16). Not by our own strength, and not by fleeing from faith.

Knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world. Key words. “Brotherhood” (adelphotēti), as in 2:17. “Throughout the world” (en tō kosmō). You are not alone. Believers everywhere face the same trials. Isolation is a weapon of the devil; knowing others suffer too brings strength.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every difficulty is a direct satanic attack, or that we should be obsessed with the devil. It means we should be alert, recognise his tactics, and resist by faith. He is a defeated enemy (3:22; Colossians 2:15).

In a sentence. Be alert and of sober mind. Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour. Resist him, standing firm in the faith, because you know that the family of believers throughout the world is undergoing the same kind of sufferings.

On a Tuesday. Where might the devil be trying to isolate or frighten you? Stand firm in faith, and connect with fellow believers this week.

verseByVerse.quote: And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

And after you have suffered a little while. Key words. “A little while” (oligon), as in 1:6. Suffering is real but temporary, compared with eternal glory (2 Corinthians 4:17).

The God of all grace. Key words. “All grace” (pasēs charitos): every kind of grace for every need: saving grace, sustaining grace, strengthening grace (4:10; 2 Corinthians 12:9).

Who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ. Key words. “Called” (kalesas): God’s effectual call (1:15; 2:9, 21; 3:9). Eternal glory: the goal of the call (Romans 8:30). God has not called us to suffering as the end, but through suffering to glory. “In Christ”: in union with him.

Will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you. Key words. “Himself” (autos, emphatic): God personally. Four verbs, piled up for assurance. “Restore” (katartisei, mend, repair, make complete, as fishermen mended nets, Mark 1:19). “Confirm” (stērixei, make firm, steady, set fast). Jesus told Peter, “When you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32), using this very word; here Peter does just that. “Strengthen” (sthenōsei, make strong). “Establish” (themeliōsei, set on a foundation). God will repair what suffering breaks, and make his people firm, strong and settled. This is the perseverance of the saints: God will finish what he started.

To him be the dominion forever and ever. Amen. Key words. “Dominion” (kratos, power, might). The devil roars, but God rules.

What it does not mean. It does not promise that suffering will end in this life. Restoration may be partial now and complete in glory. But it is certain.

In a sentence. And the God of all grace, who called you to his eternal glory in Christ, after you have suffered a little while, will himself restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast. To him be the power for ever and ever. Amen.

For worship. Pray this promise back to God today: “You yourself will restore, confirm, strengthen and establish me.” Then trust him to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son. Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.

By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him. Key words. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion on the second missionary journey (Acts 15:40; 16:19–25; 1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). “By” (dia, through): he may have been Peter’s secretary, helping with the polished Greek, or the bearer of the letter, or both.

I have written briefly to you. Key words. “Briefly” (di’ oligōn, in few words), as in Hebrews 13:22.

Exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Key words. “Exhorting” (parakalōn) and “declaring” (epimartyrōn, testifying). “This” is everything in the letter: the gospel of grace, including suffering for Christ. “True grace” (alēthē charin): genuine grace. Suffering does not mean grace has failed; it is part of God’s true grace.

Stand firm in it. Key words. “Stand firm” (stēte, stand). The summary of the letter: hold your ground in God’s grace.

She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings. Key words. “She”: the church, God’s chosen lady (2 John 1). “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome, as in Revelation 14:8; 17:5; 18:2. Like Babylon of old, Rome was the great world empire, the capital of idolatry and the place of exile for God’s people. Early tradition places Peter in Rome at the end of his life, where he was martyred under Nero. “Likewise chosen” (syneklektē, chosen together with you), echoing 1:1.

And so does Mark, my son. Key words. John Mark, who had once deserted Paul (Acts 13:13) and was later restored (2 Timothy 4:11). Peter’s spiritual son. Early tradition (Papias) says Mark’s Gospel records Peter’s preaching. Peter had stayed at Mark’s mother’s house in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12).

Greet one another with the kiss of love. Key words. “Kiss of love” (philēmati agapēs): the customary greeting among family members, used in the early church as a sign of family affection (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20). The form may vary by culture; the warmth should not.

Peace to all of you who are in Christ. Key words. “Peace” (eirēnē), the Hebrew shalom. For suffering exiles, the last word is peace, found “in Christ.”

What it does not mean. “Babylon” does not refer to the literal city in Mesopotamia, which was largely deserted by then. Nor does Peter’s presence in Rome establish a papacy; it shows he served there and died there as a faithful witness.

In a sentence. With the help of Silas, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly, encouraging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you her greetings, and so does my son Mark. Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.

For worship. Thank God that his grace is true, even in suffering. Stand firm in it today, and receive his peace.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. “Babylon” is very probably a code name for Rome. Mark is John Mark, whom early tradition links with Peter as the source of Mark’s Gospel.

Amen.<sup>12</sup>By Silvanus, a faithful brother as I regard him, I have written briefly to you, exhorting and declaring that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.<sup>13</sup>She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, my son.<sup>14</sup>Greet one another with the kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.
